title: Daodejing, chapter 5 (Mawangdui silk manuscripts)
language: Classical Chinese (silk transcription; received text) / English
source: Mawangdui Laozi A and B silk manuscripts (plates of Changsha Mawangdui Han mu jianbo jicheng vol. 1, via Wikimedia Commons) + Wikisource column transcription + Wang Bi received text (Wikisource) + Legge 1891 English (Project Gutenberg)
description: Daodejing chapter 5 as written on the two Mawangdui silk manuscripts of the Laozi (before 168 BCE), with Legge's English and the received Chinese text.
introduction:
Chapter 5 of the Daodejing (Laozi), shown on the two oldest nearly complete copies of the work: the silk manuscripts Laozi A and Laozi B, found in 1973 in Tomb 3 at Mawangdui, Changsha (Hunan), a tomb sealed in 168 BCE. Laozi A is written in a script between seal and clerical forms and does not avoid the personal name of the Han founder Liu Bang (邦); it is commonly dated before 195 BCE. Laozi B is in clerical script, avoids 邦, and is commonly dated 194-180 BCE. Both put the De part (chapters 38-81) before the Dao part (chapters 1-37), and a few chapters stand in a different order from the received text.

Each section gives the silk transcription column by column, with the Jicheng column number before each column (for Laozi B, 上 and 下 are the upper and lower halves of a column, photographed on facing plates), and links to the plate that carries those columns. □ marks a lost character; ∠, ‧ and ﹦ are marks written on the silk (﹦ repeats the character before it). Below the transcription is the received text of the Wang Bi recension, which is the text James Legge translated in 1891; the silk wording differs from it, most visibly in 恆 for received 常 (the received text avoids the name of Emperor Wen, Liu Heng), in the frequent final particle 也, and in loan characters such as 胃 for 謂.
translator_notes: English: James Legge, The Tao Teh King (Sacred Books of the East 39, 1891); Legge's paragraph numbers are kept as superscripts.
Legge translated the received text, not the silk manuscripts. Where the silk wording differs, his English follows the received text shown under the transcription.
Silk transcription: Wikisource Page transcriptions of the Jicheng plates (revisions of 18 October 2026, marked not yet proofread on Wikisource), checked against the plates for each chapter opening.

translation.original_ref: Daodejing 5; Mawangdui Laozi A (甲本) col. 101 to 102; Jicheng vol. 1 plate p. 99
translation.original_text:
101天地不仁以萬物為芻狗∠聲人不仁∠以百省□□
102狗天地□間□猶橐籥輿虛而不淈動而俞出多聞數窮不若守於中
translation.edition_text: 天地不仁，以萬物為芻狗；聖人不仁，以百姓為芻狗。天地之間，其猶橐籥乎？虛而不屈，動而愈出。多言數窮，不如守中。
translation.text:
1Heaven and earth do not act from (the impulse of) any wish to be benevolent; they deal with all things as the dogs of grass are dealt with. The sages do not act from (any wish to be) benevolent; they deal with the people as the dogs of grass are dealt with.

2May not the space between heaven and earth be compared to a bellows?

'Tis emptied, yet it loses not its power;
'Tis moved again, and sends forth air the more.
Much speech to swift exhaustion lead we see;
Your inner being guard, and keep it free.
translation.scan_note: Laozi A (甲本), columns 101 to 102, on plate p. 99 of Changsha Mawangdui Han mu jianbo jicheng, vol. 1 (column numbers are printed under each plate; the columns run from right to left). Checked on the image: column 101 reads 象帝之先 天地不仁以萬物為芻狗 (the opening of this chapter, with the end of the preceding text where shown). □ marks a character lost on the silk (4 in this section). Transcription and column numbers: Wikisource 老子 (帛書甲本), which follows the Jicheng column numbering. The English is Legge's translation of the received text, shown below the silk transcription; the silk wording differs from it in many places, so compare the two Chinese texts for the variants.
